title: Java Streams, Lambdas and Optional: Quick Revision
summary: Night-before revision notes on Java functional interfaces, lambdas, method references, the Stream pipeline, collectors, laziness and Optional. Covers the mental model, core usage, comparisons, common mistakes and a closing cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Functional Interfaces, Lambdas and Method References
points: Functional interface = exactly one abstract method (default/static/Object methods don't count); @FunctionalInterface makes the compiler enforce it

Core java.util.function types: Function<T,R> apply, Predicate<T> test, Consumer<T> accept, Supplier<T> get, UnaryOperator<T>, BinaryOperator<T>; primitive variants (IntFunction, ToIntFunction) avoid boxing
Lambda syntax (a, b) -> expr or { stmts; return x; }; target type is inferred from the context, and the lambda captures only effectively final locals
Four method reference kinds: static (Integer::parseInt), bound instance (System.out::println), unbound instance (String::length), constructor (ArrayList::new)

Interview Point: Why must captured locals be effectively final? How does a lambda differ from an anonymous class (this, compiled form)? When is String::length unbound versus System.out::println bound?

chapters.title: The Stream Pipeline: Source, Intermediate, Terminal
points: A stream is a one-shot view over a source that does not store data or modify the source; a pipeline = source → zero or more intermediate ops → exactly one terminal op
Sources: collection.stream(), Arrays.stream(arr), Stream.of(...), Stream.iterate/generate (infinite, need limit), IntStream.range(0, n)
Intermediate ops return a Stream: filter, map, flatMap, distinct, sorted, limit, skip, peek; stateful ones (sorted, distinct) must see all the data
Terminal ops produce a result or side effect: collect, forEach, count, reduce, findFirst, anyMatch/allMatch/noneMatch, toList() (Java 16+, unmodifiable)
Example: names.stream().filter(n -> n.length() > 3).map(String::toUpperCase).sorted().toList()
Interview Point: Intermediate vs terminal op, and how to tell them apart? Can a stream be reused? Stateless vs stateful intermediate ops?

chapters.title: map, filter, reduce and Laziness
points: map transforms 1:1 (Function), filter keeps elements where the Predicate is true, flatMap flattens each element's stream into one (1:N): List<List<T>> → Stream<T>
reduce(identity, BinaryOperator) returns T; reduce(BinaryOperator) returns Optional<T>; the op must be associative and the identity neutral for parallel streams to be correct
Laziness: intermediate ops run nothing until a terminal op is called; no terminal op means no execution (a peek or map with print never fires)
Elements flow one at a time through the whole pipeline (vertical processing), not stage by stage; short-circuit ops (findFirst, anyMatch, limit) stop early, even on infinite streams
Primitive streams: mapToInt(...).sum()/average()/max() avoid boxing; boxed() converts back to Stream<Integer>
Interview Point: Why does a stream with only filter and map print nothing? What is the order of peek output for two chained ops? map vs flatMap, and reduce vs collect?

chapters.title: Collectors: groupingBy, toMap and More
points: collect(Collectors.toList()/toSet()) is mutable reduction; toList() on a Stream is unmodifiable; joining(", ", "[", "]") builds a String
groupingBy(classifier) returns Map<K, List<T>>; a downstream collector changes the value: groupingBy(Emp::dept, counting()) / summingInt / mapping(Emp::name, toList()) / averagingDouble
partitioningBy(predicate) always gives a Map<Boolean, List<T>> with both true and false keys present, unlike groupingBy
toMap(keyFn, valueFn) throws IllegalStateException on duplicate keys; fix with a merge function toMap(k, v, (a, b) -> a); a null value throws NPE; pass a 4th arg (TreeMap::new) for the map type
groupingBy(f, TreeMap::new, downstream) sets the map type; the default is an unordered HashMap, so don't rely on order
Interview Point: groupingBy vs partitioningBy? What happens when toMap hits duplicate keys? How do you count per group or get a map of sums?

chapters.title: Optional and Common Stream Mistakes
points: Optional<T> is a container that is either empty or holds a value, meant as a return type to signal 'maybe no result'; create with of (NPE on null), ofNullable, empty
Consume safely: orElse(default) evaluates its argument eagerly, orElseGet(supplier) is lazy, orElseThrow(), ifPresent(consumer), ifPresentOrElse; map/flatMap/filter chain without null checks
Avoid get() without isPresent; don't use Optional for fields, parameters or collections, and never return null from an Optional-returning method
Reusing a consumed stream throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed; create a new stream per use

Mistakes: mutating external state inside map/forEach (not thread-safe in parallel), modifying the source mid-pipeline (ConcurrentModificationException), using parallel() on small or I/O-bound work, and relying on peek for logic
Interview Point: orElse vs orElseGet difference? Why is Optional not for fields or parameters? Why is a stream not reusable?

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: Lambdas, Streams, Collectors, Optional
points: Functional interfaces: Function T→R, Predicate T→boolean, Consumer T→void, Supplier ()→T, UnaryOperator T→T, BinaryOperator (T,T)→T
Pipeline: source → intermediate (lazy: filter, map, flatMap, sorted, distinct, limit) → terminal (collect, reduce, count, forEach, findFirst, anyMatch)
Collectors: toList, toSet, joining, groupingBy(f, downstream), partitioningBy(p), toMap(k, v, merge), counting, summingInt, mapping
Optional: ofNullable, map, filter, orElseGet (lazy) over orElse (eager), orElseThrow, ifPresentOrElse; avoid get()
Gotchas: a stream is single-use, nothing runs without a terminal op, toMap duplicate keys throw, lambdas capture effectively final locals only, no side effects in stream ops
Interview Point: Walk through the pipeline order for filter→map→collect on 3 elements; pick the right collector for 'count employees per department'; spot the bug in a reused stream
